newsitem.title: USA: Fran heads toward U.S. as Category 2 hurricane.
newsitem.headline: Fran heads toward U.S. as Category 2 hurricane.

text.p: A hurricane warning was posted for the northwestern Bahamas on Tuesday as Hurricane Fran gained strength and edged across the Atlantic toward the United States, the National Hurricane Center said.

At 5 p.m. EDT (2100 GMT) Fran was near latitude 25.4 north and longitude 72.9 west, or about 285 miles (460 km) east of Nassau, Bahamas, and moving west-northwest near 13 mph (20 kmh), a path that forecasters said could bring the storm to the United States on Thursday.
"A hurricane watch could be issued for a portion of the southeast United States tonight or Wednesday," said Ed Rappaport, a hurricane specialist at the National Hurricane Center.

Although the storm was several hundred miles (kms) east of the Florida coast, at a latitude just south of Miami, forecasters said they were expecting a gradual turn toward the northwest during the next 24 hours, diminishing Fran's threat to the heavily populated southern portion of the state.

"If this (northwest turn) actually is realized, which we think it will, it will lessen the chances of landfall in the southern Florida region and increase the chances in the north Florida to the North Carolina region, and that would be two to three days out," said Bill Frederick, a meteorologist at the National Hurricane Center.

Fran's maximum sustained winds increased as it moved over warmer water, reaching about 105 mph (165 kmh) by 5 p.m. EDT (2100 GMT). That strengthening made Fran a strong Category 2 hurricane capable of considerable damage to mobile homes, vegetation and piers. More strengthening was expected before Fran made landfall.

A hurricane warning was in effect for the sparsely populated islands of the northwestern Bahamas as Fran's path paralleled north of the island chain. A hurricane watch, indicating hurricane conditions -- maximum sustained winds of 74 mph (119 km) or higher -- was expected within 36 hours, and a tropical storm warning, indicating that winds of 39 to 73 mph (63-117 kph) might arrive within 24 hours, was in effect in the central Bahamas from Acklins Island to Cat Island.

The Club Med in the Bahamian island San Salvador closed its beach on Tuesday as Fran generated high waves and brisk winds. With rough seas, heavy rain and active thunderstorms expected as Fran's edge brushed the islands, residents of Abaco, Cat Island and Eleuthera were advised to stay indoors.

"Depending upon the speed of the storm we're looking to meet sometime Thursday afternoon. If it starts to make funny changes we're going to meet sooner," said Clarence Skinner, head of the emergency control group in Dare County, North Carolina, noting that Fran would only get stronger as it moved over warm ocean waters.
"There's a high probability of it being a Category 3 when it comes to shore," he said.

In Dare County, which encompasses Cape Hatteras on North Carolina's Outer Banks, "no swimming" advisories were lifted at beaches on Tuesday for the first time since Edouard threatened the state late last week.
Edouard was declared extra-tropical before dawn on Tuesday as it moved in the north Atlantic southwest of Halifax, Nova Scotia.
